questions.question_text: A couple wants to save $\$24\,000$ in $5\text{ years}$ for a trip by depositing an equal amount at the end of each year into an account paying $6\%$ p.a. compounded annually. Calculate the required annual deposit.

options.why: Divided $\$24\,000$ by 5 years, ignoring compound interest earned.
Calculated payment using start-of-period compounding (annuity due) formula.
Divided by $(1.06)^5$ instead of using the geometric series annuity divisor.

questions.question_text: A business needs $\$100\,000$ in $4\text{ years}$ to purchase new servers. Equal deposits are made at the end of each quarter into a fund earning $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly. Find the quarterly deposit $a$.

options.why: Divided $\$100\,000$ into 16 equal quarterly parts without accounting for interest.
Treated the quarterly payments as being made at the beginning of each quarter.
Used $n = 4$ years instead of $n = 16$ quarterly compounding periods.

questions.question_text: Zack deposits $\$350$ at the end of each month into an annuity earning $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. How many whole months will it take for the balance to first exceed $\$15\,000$?

options.why: Rounded down from $38.48$, which yields a balance strictly below $\$15\,000$.
Divided $\$15\,000$ by $\$350$ without accounting for monthly compound interest.
Used the annual interest rate of $6\%$ instead of the monthly rate of $0.5\%$.

questions.question_text: Deposits of $\$1500$ are made at the end of each year into an investment account earning $7\%$ p.a. compounded annually. Find the number of whole years required to reach a target of $\$30\,000$.

options.why: Truncated $12.78$ years to $12$, which leaves the fund short of the $\$30\,000$ target.
Divided $\$30\,000$ by $\$1500$ without including compound interest.
Subtracted $1$ on the wrong side when rearranging the logarithm expression.

questions.question_text: Option X deposits $\$800$ per quarter for $6\text{ years}$ at $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly. Option Y deposits $\$400$ per quarter for $12\text{ years}$ at $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly. Both deposit $\$19\,200$ in total. What is the difference in future values?

options.why: Assumed identical future values because total deposits are both $\$19\,200$.
Calculated future values assuming payments were made at the start of each quarter (annuity due).
Calculated future values using annual compounding with annualised deposits instead of quarterly.

questions.question_text: An investor deposits $\$600$ at the end of each month into an annuity for $10\text{ years}$. How much additional money is accumulated if the interest rate is $7.2\%$ p.a. compounded monthly instead of $4.8\%$ p.a. compounded monthly?

options.why: Calculated the simple interest difference ($72\,000 \times 0.024 \times 10$).
Calculated annuity due start-of-month differences instead of ordinary annuity.
Used annual compounding with annualised deposits instead of monthly compounding.

questions.question_text: A municipality plans to accumulate $\$1\,200\,000$ in a sinking fund over $15\text{ years}$ to build a recreation centre. Interest is $5.4\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. Calculate the monthly contribution $a$ required at the end of each month.

options.why: Divided total target by 180 months without accounting for compound interest.
Calculated payments using start-of-month payments (annuity due) formula.
Used annual periods of $15$ rather than monthly periods of $180$.

questions.question_text: A fund with monthly contributions of $\$450$ earns $6.6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. How many additional whole months does it take to grow the fund from $\$50\,000$ to $\$100\,000$ compared to growing from $\$0$ to $\$50\,000$?

options.text: It takes $28$ fewer months to reach the second $\$50\,000$.
It takes the exact same number of months because the dollar increment is the same.
options.why: Ignored compound interest earned on the existing $\$50\,000$ balance.

options.text: It takes $14$ more months to reach the second $\$50\,000$.
options.why: Assumed diminishing returns on compounding over time.

options.text: It takes $42$ fewer months because interest doubles every year.
options.why: Overestimated the acceleration of compound interest.

questions.solution_text:
$r = \dfrac{0.066}{12} = 0.0055$
For $\$50\,000$:
$50000 = 450\left[\dfrac{1.0055^{n}-1}{0.0055}\right] \implies 1.0055^{n_{1}} = 1.611111 \implies n_{1} \approx 87.03 \implies 88\text{ months}$
For $\$100\,000$:
$100000 = 450\left[\dfrac{1.0055^{n}-1}{0.0055}\right] \implies 1.0055^{n_{2}} = 2.222222 \implies n_{2} \approx 145.60 \implies 146\text{ months}$
Time for second $\$50\,000 = 146 - 88 = 58\text{ months}$
$\text{Difference} = 88 - 58 = 28\text{ fewer months}$
